title: DeSantis Blames Midterm Rout on GOP Failure to 'Shut Off H-1B Visas'
excerpt: Florida's governor called the Republican defeat 'close to an extinction-level event' and faulted Senate Republicans for not ending the H-1B programme — the route used by most Indian tech professionals in the US — while they held Congress.
body:
• Florida Governor Ron DeSantis blamed Senate Republicans for the party's midterm defeat, asking why they had not acted to "shut off H-1B visas" or codify President Trump's immigration executive orders while Republicans held Congress.
  • Republicans lost control of both the House and the Senate in the November 3 elections; with Democrats set to control Congress from January, legislation to eliminate the H-1B programme is effectively off the table in the near term.
  • India-born workers received 70 per cent of the roughly 406,000 H-1B petitions approved in fiscal 2025, according to the USCIS annual report to Congress released in April — and about 78 per cent of approvals for continuing employment.
  • No immigration rule changed this week: H-1B petitions continue under the existing USCIS H-1B rules, including the $100,000 payment that applies to certain new petitions filed on or after September 21, 2025 for beneficiaries outside the United States without a valid H-1B visa.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has faulted Senate Republicans for failing to curb the H-1B visa programme, the main route by which Indian technology professionals work in the United States, as he blamed the party's midterm losses partly on its own voters staying home.

Republicans lost control of both the House and the Senate on Tuesday, November 3. At a news conference in Florida on Wednesday, DeSantis called the results "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country, as we have seen probably in the last 100 years," according to reporting by BizzBuzz and Fox News.

What DeSantis said

Asked by Fox News host Laura Ingraham how big a mistake it was not to get rid of the Senate filibuster, DeSantis said he "saw no indication that the current group of Republican senators were interested in doing that type of conservative change." He then listed what he presented as missed immigration action.

"Why haven't we done immigration, shut off H-1B visas? Why haven't we codified Trump's immigration executive orders?"

— Ron DeSantis, Governor of Florida

DeSantis also asked why Republicans had not "stripped jurisdiction from the federal courts over deportation cases," adding: "There's so many things that could have been done, they didn't even attempt it."

His explanation for the scale of the defeat was two-sided. The result was, he said, "a rebuke of the president and the Congress by Democrats, independents and some Republicans that crossed over." But, he added, "a lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate." He singled out Texas, long described as "the crown jewel of Republican politics," where Republicans lost a highly publicised US Senate race and statewide offices including governor and attorney general. "If the Republican Party doesn't have Texas as an anchor, then we're not gonna be viable nationally going forward," he said. Republican Byron Donalds won the race to succeed DeSantis as Florida governor, Fox News reported.

Why H-1B sits at the centre of the argument

The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign nationals in specialty occupations, largely in technology. It is capped at 65,000 new visas a year, plus 20,000 for holders of US advanced degrees. Indians are by far its largest beneficiaries: according to the latest annual report to Congress by US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), released in April, 70 per cent of the roughly 406,000 H-1B petitions approved in fiscal year 2025 were for beneficiaries born in India, with China a distant second at about 12 per cent.

That is why a call to "shut off" the programme lands directly on Indian professionals and their employers. Ending the programme, however, is not something a governor or a president can do by announcement: it would require legislation from Congress, which Democrats will control from January.

What this means for Indian professionals

For current H-1B holders and applicants, DeSantis's remarks change no rule, deadline or fee. As our earlier reporting noted, lawyers say the midterm result brings no immediate H-1B relief either — the programme continues on its existing terms, and readers should follow the USCIS H-1B Specialty Occupations page for the rules that actually govern a petition, including the $100,000 payment attached to certain petitions filed on or after September 21, 2025. The practical effect of the election runs the other way from DeSantis's complaint: a Democratic Congress makes near-term legislation against H-1B highly unlikely.

A recurring theme, and what happens next

DeSantis, who leaves office in January and has not ruled out a 2028 presidential run, has made H-1B a recurring target. At an event near Lakeland on September 14, he said: "I think we should eliminate H-1B visas in the United States, to be quite frank." His post-election remarks keep the issue in his national argument even as the congressional path to acting on it closes.

What to watch is positioning, not policy: whether other Republicans take up the same charge as the party absorbs the midterm result, and whether H-1B features in early 2028 campaigning. The visa programme itself enters 2027 unchanged by this week's politics.
